messages.content: Our rookie is hitting .350 three weeks into the season. The broadcast keeps calling him a future batting champion. Should I believe the .350?

Believe that he has hit .350 so far. Do not believe he IS a .350 hitter yet — those are different claims, and the gap between them is measurable.

He has about 40 at-bats. For a batting average, the standard error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n). At p = .350 and n = 40: sqrt(0.35 x 0.65 / 40) = sqrt(0.00569) ≈ .075. One standard error is 75 points of batting average. A rough 95% range is .350 plus or minus .148 — somewhere between a .200 hitter and a .500 hitter. Forty at-bats cannot tell those apart.

Now give him 400 at-bats at the same .350: the standard error falls to sqrt(0.2275/400) ≈ .024, and the range tightens to roughly .303 to .397. Same average, completely different information.

The honest sentence is: he has had a hot three weeks, and hot three weeks are what .260 hitters and .330 hitters both produce regularly. Check back at 300 at-bats.
Our goalie has a .950 save percentage over his last six games and the announcers say he's 'seeing the puck like a beach ball.' His career number is .915. Has he leveled up?

Almost certainly not — or rather, six games cannot show it either way.

Six games is roughly 180 shots faced. If his true talent were still .915, the standard error on 180 shots is sqrt(0.915 x 0.085 / 180) ≈ .021. His observed .950 sits (0.950 - 0.915) / 0.021 ≈ 1.7 standard errors above his career rate. That is the kind of deviation ordinary luck produces in a .915 goalie every few months — noticeable, not remarkable.

Two more cautions. Shot quality varies: 180 shots against weak offenses from long range are not 180 average shots, and save percentage does not adjust for that. And the six games were chosen because they are his best six — nobody computes a goalie's percentage over an arbitrary six games in February. Selecting the window after seeing the results guarantees the window looks special.

Goalies do have real hot and cold stretches in the trivial sense that pucks went in or did not. Claiming a new level needs a few hundred more shots, not a narrative.
Analysts talk about stats 'stabilizing.' Why does a hitter's strikeout rate become meaningful in a few weeks but his batting average takes a year or more?

Because stabilization is about how much of what you observe is signal and how much is dice, and that ratio differs enormously by stat.

Every plate appearance gives you a strikeout verdict — he struck out or he did not — and the outcome depends mostly on the hitter's own approach, which is stable. Researchers who compute stabilization points (the sample where observed variance splits roughly half skill, half noise) find strikeout rate gets there in a matter of weeks of plate appearances.

Batting average is polluted by what happens after contact: whether a ground ball finds a hole, whether a liner is caught at the wall. The hitter controls the swing; he barely controls the landing spot. So each at-bat carries far less information about his true batting talent, and the literature puts batting average's stabilization point at a full season of at-bats or beyond. Batting average on balls in play is worse still — on the order of multiple seasons.

The practical rule: early in the season, trust the stats that describe what the player did (strikeouts, walks, exit velocity) and distrust the stats that describe what happened to him (average, and especially average on balls in play). The broadcast almost always does the reverse, because what happened makes the better story.
A young guard is shooting 45% from three this year and an older star is at 38%. My friend says the kid is simply the better shooter now. The kid has taken 60 threes, the star 600. Who's right?

Your friend is comparing two numbers with wildly different amounts of evidence behind them.

Standard error for the kid: sqrt(0.45 x 0.55 / 60) ≈ .064 — his 45% comes with about 6.4 points of uncertainty per standard error, so his true talent could plausibly be anywhere from the low 30s to the high 50s.

For the star: sqrt(0.38 x 0.62 / 600) ≈ .020 — two points of uncertainty. His 38% is close to a settled fact about him.

There is a second effect pushing the same direction: league average from three is in the mid-30s, and a rational estimate for a player with only 60 attempts pulls his observed 45% a long way toward that league figure, because most players are near it. The star's 600 attempts barely move.

So the honest ranking is: the star is a proven ~38% shooter; the kid is an unknown who has had 60 good attempts. He might genuinely be better. Sixty shots cannot establish it, and anyone stating it flatly is reading tea leaves with decimals.
Our new quarterback is completing 71% of his passes through three games. The show this morning asked if he's already elite. Three games, about 100 attempts. Verdict?

Three games is a trailer, not the movie.

On 100 attempts, the standard error of a completion percentage is sqrt(0.65 x 0.35 / 100) ≈ .048 — nearly five points. If his true talent were a thoroughly ordinary 65%, seeing 71% or better over some 100-attempt stretch would be unremarkable; if his true talent were 71%, seeing 65% would be equally ordinary. The sample cannot separate 'elite' from 'average guy, good month.'

Give him a full season of roughly 550 attempts and the standard error shrinks to about .020. Then 71% would mean something real, because an average quarterback almost never sustains it for 550 throws.

Also note what the three games hide: opponent quality, drops credited to no one, and the fact that we are discussing him precisely because the number is high. Quarterbacks who start at 58% do not get segments. The question 'is he elite?' is only ever asked about the ones whose small samples landed high — which is most of why the answer, a month later, is usually 'not yet.'
Our striker has 8 goals on 30 shots this season — a 27% conversion rate. His career rate is 15%. The commentator says his finishing has 'gone to another level.' Has it?

The commentator is describing 30 coin flips as a transformation.

If his true finishing talent were unchanged at 15%, the standard error on 30 shots is sqrt(0.15 x 0.85 / 30) ≈ .065. His observed 27% is about 1.8 standard errors above his career rate. That happens by chance alone in a meaningful minority of 30-shot stretches — and a top-league season contains dozens of strikers, so several of them will post a stretch like this every year without improving at all.

There is a better tool for exactly this question: expected goals. If those 30 shots were worth, say, 7.5 xG, then 8 goals is nearly perfect agreement with the chances he had — the story is chance creation, not finishing. If they were worth 4 xG, he has genuinely run hot on finishing, which is the part of performance that historically persists the least.

Finishing skill exists, but it reveals itself over hundreds of shots. Thirty shots can show you a highlight reel. They cannot show you a new level.
A reliever has a 3.00 ERA after 30 innings. How much should I trust that as his true level?

Very little, and we can put a number on 'little.'

A 3.00 ERA over 30 innings means 10 earned runs allowed. Runs arrive roughly like a counting process, and for counting processes the noise scales with the square root of the count: sqrt(10) ≈ 3.2 runs. So his run total is 10 plus or minus about 3.2 per standard error, before we even argue about defense, park, or inherited runners.

Convert the 95% range back to ERA: 10 runs plus or minus 6.3 gives a range of about 3.7 to 16.3 earned runs, which over 30 innings is an ERA between roughly 1.10 and 4.90. Thirty innings in, this pitcher is statistically consistent with being excellent and with being below average. Both. Simultaneously.

This is why ERA needs hundreds of innings to speak clearly, and why smart evaluation of a reliever leans on the components that stabilize faster — strikeouts, walks, ground balls — over a number that is 10 events wearing a ratio's clothing. When a broadcast calls a reliever 'a 3.00 ERA guy' in May, it is naming his luck so far, not his talent.
The graphic says our guard is a 90% free-throw shooter this season. He's attempted 50. Is he really a 90% shooter?

He has made 90% of 50. Whether he IS a 90% shooter is a claim 50 attempts cannot carry.

The standard error is sqrt(0.90 x 0.10 / 50) ≈ .042 — about four points. So his true talent is plausibly anywhere from the low 80s to the mid 90s. A true 84% shooter — good, not historic — will shoot 90% or better over a given 50-attempt stretch fairly often, and there are hundreds of guards taking 50 free throws a season, so some of them post a gaudy percentage every year.

True 90% free-throw shooters are vanishingly rare across a career; the prior should be skeptical. Watch what happens over the next 200 attempts: if he is a genuine 90% shooter he will stay near it, and if he is an 84% shooter having a charmed season, the percentage will melt toward the low 80s — not because he got worse, but because the estimate got honest.

The graphic is not lying. It is just answering a smaller question than the one you are asking.
A winger is shooting 20% this season — 16 goals on 80 shots. His career shooting percentage is 11%. Breakout, or something else?

Start with the arithmetic, then with the league.

If his true talent were still 11%, the standard error on 80 shots is sqrt(0.11 x 0.89 / 80) ≈ .035. His 20% is about 2.6 standard errors high. For this one player, named in advance, that would be mildly surprising — roughly a 1-in-100 stretch.

But he was not named in advance. He was named because he is the one at 20%. A league has several hundred forwards taking 80 shots; if every one of them were an unchanged 11% shooter, pure chance would still park a handful of them 2.5 standard errors or more above their talent by midseason. The broadcast then profiles whichever ones chance selected, and the profile always finds a reason — a new stick, a new linemate, a summer of training.

Hockey shooting percentage is one of the least persistent stats in sports at the individual level; team shot quality and plain puck luck dominate a half-season. The honest forecast: his percentage falls toward the low teens, his goal pace slows, and the 'breakout' segment is quietly never mentioned again. If he is still at 18% after 250 shots, come back and we will talk about a real change.

A golfer made 13 of 20 putts from eight feet at this week's tournament. The coverage said his putting is 'dialled in' — tour pros only make about half of those. Is 13 of 20 evidence he's putting better than the field?

It is evidence he made 13 putts. As evidence about his putting skill this week versus the field's, it is remarkably thin.

Tour pros make roughly half their putts from eight feet — call it a coin flip. The standard error on 20 flips is sqrt(0.5 x 0.5 / 20) ≈ .112, about 11 percentage points. Making 65% instead of 50% is only about 1.3 standard errors above the coin-flip rate. A completely average putting week produces 13-of-20 or better quite regularly; run 150 golfers through a tournament and several will post exactly this line with nothing dialled anywhere.

Putting is also the highest-variance skill in golf week to week, which is why last week's putting hero is this week's cautionary tale so often. The strokes-gained putting leaderboard reshuffles constantly, and a player would need several hundred measured putts before his putting estimate separates from the pack.

None of this denies he is putting well in the only sense that matters for this trophy — the putts dropped. But 'the putts dropped for three days' is a description of fortune, and dressing it as a skill diagnosis is how broadcasts turn weather into character.
My team has scored 24 goals from chances worth 15.2 expected goals over 12 matches. Fans say our finishing is elite and sustainable. What do the numbers actually say?

They say your team has finished well for 12 matches. 'Sustainable' is doing heavy lifting the data cannot support.

Goals are count data, and counts carry noise on the order of their square root: sqrt(24) ≈ 4.9 goals. Scoring 24 against an expectation of 15.2 is an excess of 8.8 goals, which is about 1.8 of those noise units. Suggestive — not nothing — but well short of proof, and that is before the selection effect: you are asking about your team because the gap is large. Across a 20-team league, some club runs an 8-goal finishing surplus over 12 matches every season by chance alone.

The deeper point is what expected goals measures. xG captures chance quality, and chance quality is the part of attacking that repeats. The gap between goals and xG is mostly finishing plus goalkeeping fortune, and year after year, teams' gaps shrink toward zero far more reliably than their xG does. The research consensus is that a team's xG is a better predictor of its future goals than its actual goals are.

So the honest fan position: enjoy the surplus, bank the points — they are real and they count — and expect the goals to cool toward the chances unless the chance creation itself improves. The table is not lying about the past. It is just a poor narrator of the future.
Our closer has converted his first 15 save chances and the broadcast called him 'automatic — he simply does not blow saves.' Is 15-for-15 really that special?

For a genuinely good closer, it is closer to routine than the broadcast suggests.

Elite closers convert around 90% of their chances. The probability of a 90% closer converting 15 straight is 0.9^15 ≈ 0.206 — about one in five. That is not a miracle; it is what you should expect from every fifth good closer in any given season, and there are thirty of them. Across a league, several closers will open a season 15-for-15 in most years without any of them being literally automatic.

Notice the asymmetry of the narrative. The 90% figure means the same closer blows roughly one in ten over a full season, so a 45-save year typically contains four or five blown saves. When the first one arrives in June, the story will become 'his command has deserted him,' and that will be exactly as wrong as 'automatic' was — both are small samples wearing costumes.

What 15-for-15 does establish: he is very probably a good closer rather than a bad one, because a 75% closer pulls off this streak only about 1 time in 75. It ranks him. It does not exempt him from arithmetic.
How many at-bats would a hitter need before we could pin down his batting average to within about ten points? It feels like a season should be plenty.

A season is not plenty. Run the numbers and it is not close.

For a true .300 hitter, the standard error of his batting average after n at-bats is sqrt(0.30 x 0.70 / n) = sqrt(0.21/n). Set the standard error to .010 — ten points of average — and solve: n = 0.21 / 0.010² = 0.21 / 0.0001 = 2,100 at-bats.

A full season is roughly 550 at-bats. So pinning a batting average to within ten points, at just one standard error of precision, takes the better part of four seasons. And ten points is a coarse target: .290 versus .310 is the difference between a regular and a star, and after one full season the standard error is still about .019 — meaning a true .290 hitter posts .310 and a true .310 hitter posts .290 within perfectly normal luck.

This is the quiet scandal inside most baseball arguments: the sport's most famous statistic needs several years of data to say what fans think it says in May. It is why front offices weight recent seasons rather than the current one, why they trust the underlying contact quality sooner than the average, and why the correct response to a two-month batting race is usually a shrug.
Is the hot hand real? I've heard the original study said it was a myth, then someone found an error in that study. What's the honest current position?

The honest position is: a small effect probably exists, it is much smaller than fans feel it is, and the history is a beautiful lesson in how subtle statistics errors can hide real things.

In 1985, Gilovich, Vallone and Tversky analyzed shooting data and found that a player's chance of making a shot after several makes was no higher than after several misses. They concluded the hot hand was a cognitive illusion — people see streaks in random sequences. For thirty years that was the textbook answer.

In 2018, Miller and Sanjurjo found a bias in that method. When you compute the proportion of hits following streaks within a finite sequence, you systematically undercount — the shots eligible to follow a streak are a biased sample (a sequence that ends in makes contributes fewer 'after a make' trials than you'd expect). Correcting the bias in the very same data flipped the estimates: a modest hot hand, on the order of a few percentage points, appeared where the original analysis had shown none.

Where that leaves us: controlled shooting studies now tend to find a small real effect. In live games it is harder to isolate, because a player who feels hot takes harder shots and defenses shade toward him — the effect can be real and still invisible in raw percentages. What is not supported is the broadcast version: that a player who has made four straight is dramatically more likely to make the next one, and the team must force him the ball. A few points of probability, yes. Destiny, no.

Both sides of the old argument were partly right: the streaks fans point to in a box score are mostly noise, and the statisticians' clean 'myth' verdict rested on a flawed calculation. Hold both facts at once and you have the literature as it stands.
A commentator said a 10-game winning streak 'proves this team has found something special.' In a league of perfectly equal teams, how often would a 10-game streak happen by pure chance?

Constantly. Chance manufactures long streaks wholesale; it just doesn't issue press releases for the teams it skips.

Take a true .500 team. The probability of winning 10 straight starting at any specified game is (1/2)^10 = 1/1024, about 0.1%. Sounds rare — until you count the starting points. A 162-game season offers 153 places a 10-game streak could begin, so one average team expects about 153/1024 ≈ 0.15 such streaks per season. Multiply by 30 teams: a league of perfect equals produces roughly four or five 10-game winning streaks every single season, guaranteed by arithmetic, no specialness required.

A related figure: in 162 coin flips, the expected longest winning run is about log2(162) ≈ 7.3 games. So an average team rattling off 8 straight should surprise no one, and 10 is only mildly beyond the expectation.

None of this proves a particular streaking team is ordinary — good teams streak more, and a 10-game run by a strong team is partly its strength showing. It proves the streak itself is weak evidence. The streak is what a season looks like from inside; the standings in September are the evidence.
A guard hit eight straight three-pointers last night and the arena lost its mind. He's a 38% shooter from three. How improbable was that, really?

For him, on those eight shots: very. For the league, this month: inevitable. Both answers are correct, and confusing them is the whole trick.

Eight straight makes from a 38% shooter, starting at a specified shot: 0.38^8 ≈ 0.000435 — about 1 in 2,300. If you had pointed at that exact shot beforehand and predicted eight straight, you'd be a prophet.

But nobody pointed beforehand. A high-volume shooter takes about 500 threes a season, giving him roughly 493 overlapping windows of eight shots; his expected number of eight-make streaks is 493 x 0.000435 ≈ 0.21 per season. Now multiply across the roughly 100 high-volume shooters in the league: you expect on the order of 20 such streaks per season, somewhere, by someone, from pure binomial chance — assuming independence, which the small hot-hand effect would nudge only slightly.

So the arena was right to enjoy it; eight straight threes is a wonderful thing to watch. The error is only in the inference: 'we witnessed a 1-in-2,300 event, therefore something mystical happened.' The 1-in-2,300 was computed after the fact, on a window selected because it happened. Pre-select the window and it is a miracle; post-select it and it is a Tuesday in a long season.
A player just reached a 20-game hitting streak and the coverage is treating it like a moon landing. Meanwhile DiMaggio's 56 is called unbreakable. Put both in perspective with actual math.

Gladly — the math separates them by orders of magnitude, which is exactly the perspective the coverage skips.

Take a solid .300 hitter with four at-bats a game. His chance of at least one hit in a game is 1 - 0.70^4 ≈ 0.76. A 20-game streak from a specified start: 0.76^20 ≈ 0.004 — about 1 in 240. But a season offers roughly 143 starting windows, so this hitter expects a 20-game streak about 0.6 times per season. Across a league full of regulars, 20-game streaks are an annual crop. Several happen most years. It is a fine achievement and a normal event.

Now DiMaggio. He hit .357 in 1941, so his per-game chance of a hit was about 1 - 0.643^4 ≈ 0.83. Raise that to the 56th power: roughly 2.8 x 10^-5 — on the order of 1 in 36,000 per specified window, even granting his elevated average and ignoring walks eating at-bats, which make it harder still. That is a different species of event: not 'rare for a player' but 'rare for the sport across decades.'

The honest framing: a 20-game streak tells you a good hitter had a good month with the hits distributed kindly. The 56 tells you why it has stood since 1941 — it sits so far in the tail that baseball has run the experiment for 80-plus years without repeating it. Treat the first as weather and the second as climate, and your sense of wonder will be correctly allocated.
My team has won 12 straight and my uncle keeps saying they're 'due for a loss.' Is there anything to that?

Your uncle is describing a debt the universe does not keep.

Suppose your team is genuinely a .600 team — strong, not magical. Its chance of losing tonight is 40%, exactly what it was before the streak, because tonight's game does not know about the previous twelve. Coins, dice, and baseball teams have no memory and no conscience; nothing accumulates that must be repaid. That is the gambler's fallacy in its Sunday clothes.

Here is the kernel of truth buried in his intuition, because there is one. The streak does tell us the team's record over the last twelve games (12-0) is a worse forecast than its talent. Over the next fifty games, a .600 team will most likely win about thirty — playing .600 ball, not 1.000 ball. So yes, losses are coming, at the normal rate for a good team. Fans experience that return to normal as 'being due,' but the mechanism is not payback; it is that 12-0 was never their true rate in the first place.

Tell your uncle: they are not due for a loss tonight. They are due for about twenty losses over the next fifty games, arriving in no particular order, some of them in bunches that will make everyone say the magic is gone. It never was magic. It was a good team, briefly photographed from its best angle.
The broadcast made a huge deal of a 14-0 run in the third quarter — 'the game has completely turned.' How often would a run like that happen if scoring were just random?

Often enough that 'the game has turned' should be the start of skepticism, not the end of analysis.

Use a deliberately crude model: a game has around 200 scoring events, and pretend each event is a fair coin for which team scores. In 200 coin flips, the expected number of runs of seven or more consecutive events by one side is roughly 0.75 — on the order of one per game. Seven straight scoring events, mostly twos, is about a 14-0 run. So the coin-flip league produces a 'momentum-shifting' 14-0 run in a typical game, sometimes two, with no momentum anywhere in the model — because the model contains nothing but coins.

Real basketball adds real effects on top: lineup changes, foul trouble, a coach's adjustment, a star heating up in the small genuine hot-hand sense. Runs can be caused. But the base rate says a big run is not, by itself, evidence of a cause. Long sequences of anything — hits, goals, points — clump naturally, and the human eye reads clumps as stories.

The tell is asymmetry of attention. The same game contains dozens of unremarkable stretches where the teams traded baskets; nobody graphs those. The run gets a name and a replay package because it is the clumpiest clump. When you hear 'this game has completely turned,' translate it as 'the random sequence just produced its most visible cluster' — and then check whether anything structural actually changed.
Our team won Game 6 by 28 points and every preview says they have 'all the momentum' going into Game 7. Does a blowout win actually carry over to the next game?

The research on this is about as clear as sports research gets: barely, if at all, once you account for the things that actually predict Game 7 — team quality and home court.

Studies of playoff series that examine whether the margin of the previous game predicts the next one find the effect is tiny compared to who is simply the better team and where the game is played. A 28-point win mostly tells you what you already knew: on that night, with those matchups and that crowd, one team was much better. The information content for Game 7 is small, because the result was already priced into our estimate of the teams.

There is also a mechanical reason blowouts overstate themselves. In a 28-point game, the losing coach benches starters early, the winner's bench plays the fourth quarter, and both teams stop optimizing for margin. The 28 points are partly a decision, not a measurement. Meanwhile the losing team gets two days of targeted adjustments — if anything, the specific things that produced the blowout are the things most likely to be addressed.

None of this means your team is not the favorite. If they were the better team all along and Game 7 is at home, they should be favored — for those reasons. 'Momentum' is the name we give to the gap between what happened last game and what we can explain. It is a label for our ignorance, and it predicts almost nothing.
It feels like every single game I watch has some incredible streak in it. Am I imagining that, or is something else going on?

Something else, and it is not your imagination failing — it is your attention succeeding at exactly the wrong job.

A basketball game contains hundreds of overlapping sequences you could draw a window around: possessions, minutes, quarters, one player's shots, one team's defensive stands. Almost all of those windows are boring. A handful, by pure chance, are extreme — a run of makes, a drought, a burst of turnovers. Your attention, and the broadcast's graphics department, find the extreme ones with perfect reliability. The game you experience is the game after that filter.

So of course every game 'has' an incredible streak. A long random sequence cannot avoid producing locally improbable patterns; improbability is guaranteed somewhere, just never at a pre-announced address. It is the same reason every long drive contains a stretch of three green cars in a row.

The corrective is to ask the pre-announcement question: before the game, would you have bet on this specific streak, by this player, in this quarter? If the answer is no — and it is always no — then what you witnessed was not an improbable event in the meaningful sense. It was an inevitable pattern, noticed.

Streaks feel like the texture of sports because they are the texture of randomness itself, and randomness is what sports are mostly made of between the skill differences. The skill is real. It is just quieter than the noise, and noise is what gets a replay.
The headline says we're 'the hottest team in baseball — 15 wins in our last 18.' We're a decent team, maybe a .550 team. How special is 15 of 18, honestly?

For one specified 18-game window: fairly special. For a league in June: completely guaranteed. The headline lives in the gap between those two statements.

For a true .550 team, the binomial probability of winning at least 15 of a given 18 games is about 1.2%. If a fortune teller had named these exact 18 games in advance, 15-3 would be impressive evidence of something.

But nobody named them in advance. A season gives each team about 145 overlapping 18-game windows, and there are 30 teams — over 4,000 team-windows a season. At 1.2% apiece, chance alone schedules dozens of '15 of 18' stretches every year. The hottest-team headline is not reporting an event; it is reporting the maximum of a very large number of draws, and the maximum of a large number of draws is always gaudy.

Notice also that the window was chosen to flatter: 18 games, not 16 or 25, because 18 is where the record peaks. Extend the window in either direction and the heat dilutes toward .550, which is the team's actual temperature.

Enjoy the wins — they count in the standings exactly like the ugly ones. Just do not let a headline convince you the team's talent changed. A .550 team that plays .550 ball the rest of the way will look like it 'cooled off.' It never heated up. The window did.
Every September, a couple of NFL teams start 3-0 and get Super Bowl talk, and every few years a team starts 8-0. Are those starts equally meaningful?

Not remotely — and the difference is a clean lesson in how evidence scales.

If all 32 teams were exactly average, each would have a (1/2)^3 = 12.5% chance of starting 3-0. Expected number of 3-0 teams in a pure-chance league: 32 x 0.125 = 4, every season. A 3-0 start is what the schedule does to a handful of ordinary teams annually. It carries almost no information.

Now 8-0. A truly average team pulls that off with probability (1/2)^8 ≈ 0.4%, so a coin-flip league expects about 0.125 such starts per season — one every eight years. But genuinely good teams change the math: a team that wins 65% of its games starts 8-0 with probability 0.65^8 ≈ 3.2%. Still not likely, but roughly eight times the average team's chance. So when an 8-0 start happens, it is much more likely to have come from the small pool of strong teams than from the large pool of average ones. That is real evidence.

The general principle: a streak's meaning grows with its length not because the universe respects round numbers, but because long streaks are the one thing mediocre teams almost never counterfeit. Three games is a rumor. Eight is a signal. The Super Bowl talk should wait for the signal.
Our sixth man is the streakiest player I've ever seen — 0-for-7 one night, 5-for-6 the next. The coach says he needs to 'find consistency.' Is he actually streakier than a normal shooter?

Probably not. What you are describing is roughly what a perfectly consistent shooter looks like, because binomial variance is clumpier than human intuition expects.

Say he is a constant 40% shooter — same probability every shot, no streaks in the mechanism at all. On a seven-shot night, his chance of going 0-for-7 is 0.6^7 ≈ 2.8%. On a six-shot night, his chance of making at least five is about 4.1%. Neither is likely on a given night — but he plays 70-odd nights a season, so each flavor of extreme shows up a few times a year by pure chance. Feast and famine are both on the schedule of a player whose underlying probability never changes.

Human beings consistently underestimate this. Shown random sequences, people judge them 'too streaky' and demand hidden causes — confidence, rhythm, a hitch in the shot. Statisticians who have tested individual players' game-to-game patterns against the binomial prediction generally find the observed streakiness is close to what chance predicts, with at most a modest excess.

None of which means the coach is wrong to want better shots. Shot selection changes the 40% itself, and that is real coaching. But 'consistency' as a character trait the player lacks is mostly a story told about variance. The honest target is raising the average, not flattening the ride — the ride flattens only when the sample grows, and by then nobody is watching individual nights anymore.
The graphic bragged that a soccer team is 'unbeaten in nine.' Impressive, right?

It depends entirely on what is hiding inside the nine — and 'unbeaten' is a word designed to stop you from asking.

Suppose the run is four wins and five draws. That is 4 x 3 + 5 = 17 points from nine games, about 1.89 per game — a strong return, roughly title-challenging pace over a season. Now suppose instead it is two wins and seven draws: 13 points, about 1.44 per game — mid-table pace, the form of a team that is hard to beat and easy to hold. Both runs are 'unbeaten in nine.' The phrase cannot tell a contender from a stalemate machine.

Draws are the camouflage. A win is worth three draws, so a team can stretch an unbeaten run almost indefinitely by playing cautiously, while a braver team with six wins and three losses in the same span — no unbeaten run to advertise — actually banked more points: 18.

The honest graphic would show points per game and the win-draw split. 'Unbeaten' survives in broadcasts because it sounds like dominance and demands no follow-up. When you see it, do the one piece of arithmetic it hopes you will skip: count the wins.
A tennis player has won 24 straight matches. The commentary treats every win in the streak as equally meaningful. Is a 24-match streak a clean measure of dominance?

It is a real achievement and a dirty measurement, because a tennis streak is not 24 repetitions of the same trial.

The surface changes: a streak that runs through the clay season is partly a statement about clay. The opposition changes: early-round opponents in small events are not the top ten waiting in semifinals. The format changes: best-of-five at a major is a sterner test than best-of-three at a tour stop. And the streak is partly self-protecting — a player on a streak gets seeded, gets byes, gets night sessions and recovery time that unseeded players do not.

There is also a selection frame around the whole conversation: we count the streak because it reached 24. The same player likely had a dozen starts to streaks that died at six or nine; those were not evidence of anything either.

A cleaner dominance measure adjusts each win for the opponent — rating systems like Elo do this, crediting a win over a top-five player far more than a routine win over a qualifier. A 24-match streak built on deep runs at big events, beating top-ten opponents across two surfaces, is a genuinely towering signal. A 24-match streak assembled at smaller events on one surface is a lesser one wearing the same number.

Streaks count events. Dominance is about which events. The number is the beginning of the evaluation, not the evaluation.

Last year's Rookie of the Year hit .310. This year he's at .275 and everyone says he's suffering a 'sophomore slump' — maybe the league figured him out, maybe he got complacent. Is there a simpler explanation?

Yes: he was never a .310 hitter, and the award itself is the proof of the mechanism.

Rookie of the Year is not given to the rookie with the best true talent. It is given to the rookie with the best observed season — which is talent plus luck, with the luck component guaranteed to be favorable, because he beat out every other rookie's talent-plus-luck for the trophy. The winner is selected precisely for having his career year and his fortune peak at the same time.

Next season his talent is roughly the same and his luck is re-rolled from the middle of the distribution. The average result is a decline that looks like a slump and requires no psychology at all. This is regression to the mean, and award winners are its most reliable victims in every field: the cover athlete, the manager of the year, the fund manager on the magazine cover. The honor certifies a peak; peaks are followed by descents by definition.

Could the league also have adjusted to him? Possibly — pitchers do attack a book on a hitter in year two, and that effect is real at the margins. But you do not need it to explain .310 becoming .275. If his true talent were .285, both seasons are ordinary draws around it. The slump narrative is a story hung on arithmetic, and the arithmetic was always going to win.

A player just had a career year in his contract year, signed a huge deal, and now fans of his new team are furious that he's 'declined.' Did he dog it after getting paid, or is something else going on?

Something else, most likely — and it was predictable on the day he signed.

A 'career year' is by definition the top of a player's distribution: the season where health, luck, opportunity, and performance peaked together. Teams bidding for him priced that peak as if it were his level. When he then plays at his actual level — good, just not career-best — the gap gets read as decline, laziness, or a man relaxing on his money. Usually it is just the distribution reasserting itself.

Researchers who have looked for a contract-year effect find at most a small one, and part of even that is mechanical: players in contract years are often finally healthy, or finally given full playing time by a team showcasing them. The larger, more reliable effect runs the other direction — the season after a peak is worse than the peak, for everyone, paid or not. It is the same regression that humbles Rookie of the Year winners, with a dollar figure attached.

The front-office lesson is to pay for the projection — age curve, underlying skills, multi-year performance — and treat the platform season as evidence about the player's ceiling, not his expectation. The fan lesson is kinder: a man can be honest, hardworking, and worth most of his contract, and still never again be the player in the highlight package that got him signed. That package was his best month, not his identity.

People keep telling me our hitter's .340 average is 'BABIP-fueled' and will crash. His batting average on balls in play is .380 and the league's is around .300. How much of his average is actually at risk?

A large, computable chunk of it. BABIP is regression to the mean's poster child because it isolates the part of hitting a batter controls least: where batted balls land.

Do the arithmetic. Over a season a hitter puts roughly 500 balls in play. At a .380 BABIP, about 190 of them fall for hits. At a still-generous .310 — above league average, crediting him with real line-drive skill — about 155 fall. That is 35 hits that exist because grounders found holes and flares dropped in front of outfielders.

Spread over a 550 at-bat season, 35 hits is about 64 points of batting average. So a .340 hitter riding a .380 BABIP is, on this component alone, playing like a .275-.285 hitter whose batted balls have been dealt kindly. Strikeouts and home runs — the parts he controls — do not regress the same way, which is why his power numbers are more trustworthy than his average.

Two refinements keep this honest. BABIP is not pure luck: hitters who scorch line drives sustain higher BABIPs than slap hitters, so his personal baseline is probably above .300. And pitchers show the mirror image — a pitcher stranding a .260 BABIP against him is borrowing the same fortune. But the direction and rough size of the correction are not in doubt. When the crash comes, it will not be a slump, a mechanical flaw, or a loss of confidence. It will be ground balls finding gloves at the normal rate, which was always the most likely future.
Is the magazine cover jinx real? It seems like every athlete who gets the cover has a bad year right after.

The jinx is real as a pattern and false as a curse. What you are watching is regression to the mean with a photoshoot.

Athletes get covers at the summit of their visibility, and the summit is reached by a peak performance — a career season, a title run, a record chase. A peak performance is talent plus everything breaking right. The following season keeps the talent and re-rolls the breaks, so the average cover athlete declines. No supernatural agent is required, and none has ever been photographed near the printing plant.

The selection runs deeper than one season. A cover is often the capstone of a multi-year rise, meaning the athlete is frequently also a year older, a year more injured, and facing opponents who have spent the offseason studying exactly him. Those are real effects stacked on the statistical one, all pushing the same direction.

Notice the jinx's perfect public relations: it is only ever invoked after a decline. Cover athletes who back it up with another great year are not evidence against the jinx; they are simply not mentioned. A curse that is credited with every failure and excused from every success is not a theory — it is a superstition with a subscription department.

If you want a genuinely useful rule from all this: any honor that selects for a peak — covers, awards, career years — is a sell signal on the future and says nothing bad about the athlete. Peaks are just expensive places to stand.
A September call-up hit .420 for us last year and the fanbase demanded he start this season. He's hitting .240 in May and everyone feels betrayed. What happened?

September happened — the most misleading month on the baseball calendar, wearing a prospect's face.

Start with the sample: .420 over a September call-up is typically 60-80 at-bats, a sample in which a genuine .250 hitter can hit .420 without anything unusual occurring. Then the context: September rosters expand, so a share of his at-bats came against minor-league call-up pitchers auditioning for next year. The competition in his highlight month was, on average, the weakest he will ever face in the majors.

Then the selection: the fanbase is not demanding jobs for the call-ups who hit .190 in September, because those Septembers were equally uninformative in the other direction and nobody remembers them. Only the hot month got a constituency.

Now he faces full-strength pitching in April and May, in cold weather, with scouts having a book on him, over a sample that is still small. His .240 now is not the truth either. The honest estimate of this player was never .420 or .240; it is something built from his minor-league record, his age, his strikeout and walk rates — the unglamorous data that was available all along.

The betrayal fans feel is real but misaddressed. They were not betrayed by the player. They were betrayed by a calendar quirk and 70 at-bats, sold to them as a coronation.

Our team won 95 games and our manager won Manager of the Year. A stats guy told me we 'should' have won 88 based on our runs scored and allowed, and that next year will hurt. Is that real or just pessimism?

It is real, it has a name, and it is one of the most reliable forecasts in baseball.

The tool is Pythagorean expectation: a team's winning percentage is well predicted by its runs scored and allowed — roughly, win% ≈ RS² / (RS² + RA²). A team that outscores opponents like an 88-win team but wins 95 has collected about seven extra wins from sequencing: bunching runs in blowouts it would have won anyway is 'wasted,' while clustering them into one-run wins is gold. That clustering is mostly luck. It does not belong to the manager, the clubhouse culture, or anyone's will.

Season after season, teams' actual wins drift toward their Pythagorean record far more than the Pythagorean record drifts toward the wins. The seven-win surplus is, on average, spent by next spring. This is also why Manager of the Year is regression's favorite award: it is typically given to the manager of the team that most overperformed its run differential, which means the award nearly guarantees a 'disappointing' follow-up that gets blamed on the same man.

Keep the nuance: a small part of the gap can be real — an elite bullpen genuinely wins more one-run games than the formula credits, because the formula cannot see leverage. But a small part of seven wins is one or two, not seven.

So the stats guy is not a pessimist. He is telling you the 95 contained about 88 wins of team and 7 wins of weather, and the weather is not under contract.
Our football team went 11-6 last year but 8-1 in one-score games. This year we're 2-4 in close games and the fans say the team 'lost its clutch gene.' What actually happened?

The clutch gene is a story told about a coin while it was landing heads.

One-score games are close to coin flips even for good teams, because by definition the teams are level late, and the outcome turns on a kick, a bounce, a flag. If close games were pure coin flips, the chance of going 8-1 or better in nine of them is (9 + 1) / 512 ≈ 2%. Rare for a specified team — but there are 32 teams, so chance alone anoints about one team a season with a record like that (0.02 x 32 ≈ 0.6 expected per year). Somebody always looks clutch.

The crucial fact is persistence: year over year, a team's record in one-score games correlates with its future close-game record only weakly. Good teams do win close games a bit more often than bad ones — being better helps everywhere — but an 8-1 mark mostly measures which side of the variance you rented. The underlying team quality shows up in point differential across all games, not in the subset that happened to end close.

So this year's 2-4 is not a lost gene; it is the same team paying the other side of the distribution, and the two seasons together — something like 10-5 in close games with a strong overall record — describe a good team accurately. Fans experience regression as betrayal because last year's luck was narrated as character. It was not character then, and its absence is not a character flaw now. It is a coin, doing what coins do, in both directions.

Our point guard shot 58% from the free-throw line in the first half of the season, hired a sports psychologist, and shot 74% in the second half. The team credits the psychologist. He's a career 68% shooter. Should they?

The psychologist may be wonderful. This evidence would look almost identical if she had done nothing at all.

Start with the anomaly that needs explaining: not the 74%, but the 58%. On roughly 90 attempts, the standard error around his career 68% is sqrt(0.68 x 0.32 / 90) ≈ .049 — about five points. His first half sat about two standard errors below his established level: a bad draw, the kind a 68% shooter hits every few seasons by chance.

When did the team intervene? At the bottom. Interventions are always hired at the bottom — nobody calls a psychologist during a normal month. And from the bottom, the most likely direction for a player's next stretch is back toward his own average, intervention or no intervention. The recovery was scheduled by arithmetic before the first session.

This is the oldest trap in performance analysis — it is how most 'turnaround' methods earn their testimonials, in sports, business, and medicine alike. To actually credit the psychologist you would need the counterfactual: what do similar players' second halves look like after identical first-half dips without one? Mostly, they look like 74%.

The fair summary: the dip was noise, the recovery was regression, and the psychologist's real contribution — confidence, routine, a calmer player — is plausible but invisible in this data. Pay her for the player's peace of mind if you like. Just do not let two halves of a season testify to causation they cannot see.
A rookie quarterback lit it up for his first four starts, then fell off hard. Everyone says 'the league got film on him.' Is that the whole story?

It is a real effect wearing the costume of the whole explanation. Two things happened at once, and the film story gets credit for both.

The adjustment effect is genuine. Coordinators do catalogue a young quarterback's tendencies — his favorite concepts, where he looks first under pressure — and take them away. Plenty of careers show a real second-act dip when the league stops being surprised.

But look at the first four starts with a statistician's eye. We are discussing this quarterback because his first four starts were brilliant — that is selection. Brilliant four-game stretches are talent plus fortune: tipped balls caught instead of intercepted, a dropped pick or two, friendly opponents. Even if the league never adjusted at all, his next four starts would almost certainly be worse, because the fortune component does not renew. Regression guarantees a fall from a peak whether or not a single coordinator opened a laptop.

You can roughly separate the two with the shape of the decline. A pure regression fall lands him at his true level — often still a decent starter. A film-driven collapse tends to be specific: the taken-away throws get forced anyway, interceptions cluster on his pet plays, and the numbers keep sinking below any plausible talent level until he adapts or sits.

Most real cases are a blend, and the honest broadcast line is boring: 'some of this is the league adjusting, some of it is that his first month was never sustainable.' It fits on no graphic. It has the advantage of being true.
A golfer won a tournament on Sunday and missed the cut the next week. The coverage called it a 'winner's hangover.' Is there a less romantic explanation?

Yes — the winner's hangover is mostly a selection effect with a press conference.

A tour event has roughly 150 entrants. The winner is, almost by construction, the player whose week sat at the very top of his personal distribution: his putting, his ball-striking, his bounces, and the draw of weather all peaked in the same four days. His true skill may be top-20 in the field, but his winning week was top-1 in fortune.

Next week his skill is unchanged and his fortune is re-drawn from the middle. The expected result for even a genuinely excellent player in a 150-man field is a finish far below first — most weeks, most great players finish outside the top 10, and missing a cut requires only a mildly poor two days. So 'won, then missed the cut' is not a paradox needing psychology. It is the modal experience of being very good at a high-variance game.

Real hangover ingredients exist at the margins — a changed schedule, media duties, celebration, a new course that fits him worse. But they are seasoning. The main course is that we selected the one player out of 150 whose dice ran hottest, then acted surprised when his next roll was ordinary.

Watch for the same shape everywhere: the award winner who 'declines,' the cover athlete who 'slumps,' the rookie who 'regresses.' Different sports, same arithmetic — the peak was the story, and the return trip is just the peak's shadow.
A coach told me he praises players after great games and rips them after bad ones, and 'it works — they always play better after I rip them.' A statistician friend rolled her eyes. Why?

Because your coach has built a machine for manufacturing false evidence, and it runs in every walk of life.

This is the famous flight-instructor problem described by Kahneman and Tversky. Instructors noticed cadets flew better after being screamed at for a bad landing and worse after being praised for a smooth one, and concluded praise harms and punishment helps. The landings, though, were partly luck. An exceptionally smooth landing is followed by a more ordinary one no matter what the instructor says; an exceptionally poor one is followed by a better one for the same reason. The feedback was irrelevant — regression did all the work, and the instructors' policy collected the credit and the blame.

Your coach's version is identical. He rips a player after the player's worst game — a game that is worst partly because of bad luck — and the next game is better, as it almost always is. He praises after the best game, and the next is worse, as it almost always is. Season after season, the pattern 'confirms' that ripping works and praise spoils, and the coach becomes more certain the longer the illusion runs.

None of this proves feedback never matters — it surely does, through information and motivation. It proves this method of judging feedback cannot detect its effect, because the outcome would look the same if the coach said nothing at all. To know whether ripping helps, you would need the counterfactual: the same bad games followed by silence. Nobody runs that experiment on their own team, which is exactly why the superstition is immortal.
Our pitcher has a 2.90 ERA but his FIP is 4.10. My co-worker says FIP is a made-up nerd stat and ERA is what actually happened. Who's right about next season?

For next season, the nerd stat usually wins — and the reason is one of the great findings of modern baseball analysis.

ERA counts everything, including the two things a pitcher controls least: whether balls in play become hits (which depends heavily on defense and luck) and the order hits arrive in (stranding runners is partly skill, largely sequence fortune). FIP deliberately counts only what the pitcher controls most directly — strikeouts, walks, hit batters, home runs — and asks what his ERA would look like with average fortune on balls in play and average sequencing.

The research behind this, going back to Voros McCracken's work on defense-independent pitching, showed that pitchers' year-to-year ERA is predicted better by their FIP-type components than by their ERA itself. A 2.90 ERA with a 4.10 FIP is the classic sell-high profile: the outcomes were kind, the underlying performance was ordinary, and next season's ERA typically lands much closer to the FIP than the FIP moves toward the ERA.

Keep two honest caveats. FIP treats all home runs alike and ignores weak contact skill, which a minority of pitchers genuinely have — some pitchers sustain better-than-average results on balls in play for years, and newer metrics try to credit that. And your co-worker has one real point: ERA is what happened, and pennants are won on what happened. If you are writing the history of last season, use ERA.

But the question was next season. For prophecy, bet on the components the pitcher owns, not the fortune he borrowed.
We started the season 20-5 and the local paper has been running 'collapse' stories since we played .500 ball for the next four months. Did the team collapse?

Almost certainly not. Do the arithmetic the paper skipped: 20-5 followed by 68-69 is an 88-74 season, a .543 team. There is a much simpler description of that season than 'great team collapses': a .543 team whose wins happened to arrive front-loaded.

Sequencing is the invisible hand here. A team's 162 games are not dealt in order of quality; a good-not-great team will have stretches where it plays .800 ball and stretches where it plays .450 ball, purely from how opponents, injuries, and one-run outcomes happen to cluster. The hot start and the mediocre four months are not two teams. They are one team, sampled unevenly.

Notice how the narrative machinery works. If the same 88 wins had been spread evenly, the story is 'solid team, wire to wire.' If the team had started 5-20 and finished hot, the story is 'they figured it out in June.' Three different characters — collapse, consistency, growth — assigned to the same underlying quality based purely on the order the wins arrived.

The full-season record is the best single estimate of what the team was, and the best forecast of what it will be. The start was the anomaly; the 'collapse' was the correction. Your paper has been writing about regression to the mean for four months without once naming it — which, to be fair, would not sell many papers.
A graphic argued our bench guard is 'actually outscoring' our starter: the starter averages 24 points a game, but the bench guy scores at 18 points per 36 minutes. Is the comparison fair?

The graphic is worse than unfair — it has the ranking backwards before you even get to the caveats.

The starter scores 24 points in about 34 minutes a night. Scale him to 36 minutes: 24 x 36/34 ≈ 25.4 points per 36. The bench player's 18 per 36 comes from scoring about 7 points in 14 minutes a night (7 x 36/14 = 18). So even on the graphic's own terms, the starter produces far more per minute: 25.4 versus 18. The per-36 framing was chosen because it sounds like an equalizer while quietly shrinking the starter's actual output from view.

Then the caveats, which all cut the same way. Per-36 assumes a player can triple his minutes at the same rate, but bench minutes are the softest minutes in basketball: against second units, often in decided games, with the defense's best stoppers resting. Fouls, fatigue, and scouting all tax the player whose minutes grow. Starters face starters, set defenses, and game plans built to stop them.

Per-36 is a legitimate tool for one narrow job: comparing two reserves, or estimating whether a young player's scoring might survive a modest role increase. Used to argue a reserve outproduces a star, it is not analysis — it is a magic trick with division.
Wilt Chamberlain averaged 50.4 points a game in 1961-62. A modern star averaging 30 gets compared to him and it looks laughable. Is the comparison as lopsided as the raw numbers suggest?

Lopsided, yes. Laughable, no — and pace is the missing variable that explains most of the gap.

Points per game is a rate with a hidden denominator: opportunities. Wilt's 1962 Warriors played at a frenetic pace — possessions weren't officially counted then, but estimates put his team around 130 possessions per 48 minutes, against roughly 100 in the modern game. He also played nearly every minute, about 48.5 a game.

Convert Wilt to a per-possession basis: 50.4 points at a pace of about 130 is roughly 50.4 x 100/130 ≈ 38.8 points per 100 team possessions. A modern star's 30 per game at a pace of 100 is 30 per 100 possessions. So the era adjustment does not dethrone Wilt — 38.8 against 30 is still a chasm — but it cuts the apparent gap from 20 points to about 9, and it does so honestly.

The same adjustment runs through his whole era: league scoring, rebounding totals (more missed shots meant more rebounds to collect), and assist numbers all inflate with pace. This is why serious cross-era comparison converts counting stats to per-possession rates and compares each player to his own league's average.

The mature conclusion is the one fans resist: Wilt was more dominant relative to his era than the modern star is relative to his, AND the raw 50.4 overstates the distance between them by about half. Both facts fit in one head. Era adjustment shrinks legends; it rarely erases them.

Our first baseman hit .300 with an .850 OPS, and a debate broke out about whether he's better than a guy on another team with the same line. Our guy plays half his games at Coors Field. Does that matter, and by how much?

It matters by roughly the size of the debate.

Coors Field, with its thin air and vast outfield, has historically inflated scoring by on the order of 10% — the exact park factor varies year to year and by statistic, but a factor around 1.10 for overall offense is the right neighborhood. A hitter who posts an .850 OPS with half his games there is, to first approximation, a .850 / 1.10 ≈ .773 OPS hitter in a neutral park. That is the difference between 'clearly above average regular' and 'fringe starter,' decided entirely by geography.

This is precisely why adjusted stats exist. OPS+ and its cousins rebuild a player's line relative to his league AND his parks, scaled so 100 is league average. A 120 OPS+ at Coors and a 120 OPS+ in a pitcher's park are already the same claim — the adjustment has done the work. Arguing from raw OPS across parks is arguing with a known bias left in.

Two honest complications: park factors are usually computed from team totals, and individual players can fit a park unusually well or badly — a dead-pull power hitter and a gap-to-gap line-drive hitter do not experience Coors identically. And the adjustment is an average over seasons; single-year park factors are noisy themselves.

But those are refinements of a correction, not arguments against making it. Identical raw lines in different parks are not identical performances, and any ranking that ignores where the games were played is measuring real estate along with hitting.
Bob Gibson's 1.12 ERA in 1968 gets called the greatest pitching season ever. A modern ace with a 2.40 ERA — how do I compare them fairly?

Compare each man to his own league first, because 1968 and today are different sports wearing the same uniforms.

1968 was the 'Year of the Pitcher' — the National League's ERA was about 2.98, offense was so suppressed that baseball lowered the mound the next season. Gibson's 1.12 against a 2.98 league means he allowed runs at about 2.98 / 1.12 ≈ 2.7 times better than the average pitcher of his day.

Now the modern ace: a 2.40 ERA in a league averaging about 4.30 is 4.30 / 2.40 ≈ 1.8 times better than his league. That is a magnificent season — and by relative dominance it is not close to Gibson's. This ratio logic is what ERA+ formalizes: Gibson's ERA+ is commonly listed around 258, while a modern 2.40 typically lands in the 170s or 180s after park adjustments.

The general principle travels well: raw ERAs across eras are nearly meaningless, because the run environment — mound height, ball, strike zone, expansion, training — moves the baseline for everyone. A 3.50 ERA in 1968 was mediocre; a 3.50 ERA in a high-offense modern season is valuable. The number stayed the same; the meaning inverted.

So yes, Gibson's season survives the fair comparison, which is the mark of the truly great ones: adjust for era and the legend usually shrinks — but his does not shrink enough to matter.
Quarterback A threw for 4,800 yards, Quarterback B for 4,200. My coworker says A is obviously the better passer. A attempted 700 passes, B attempted 520. Settle it.

Your coworker has crowned the busier man, not the better one.

Per attempt: A gained 4800/700 ≈ 6.86 yards per throw; B gained 4200/520 ≈ 8.08. B produced over a yard more every time he dropped back — across a season that is an enormous efficiency gap. A's total is a volume trophy: his offense simply asked him to throw 180 more times, often because it was trailing.

Now add the tax raw totals ignore: sacks. Say A was sacked 40 times for 260 lost yards and B 25 times for 170. Net yards per dropback: A = (4800 - 260) / (700 + 40) ≈ 6.14; B = (4200 - 170) / (520 + 25) ≈ 7.39. The gap survives the adjustment and it is the honest one, because a sack is a failed pass play and belongs in the passer's ledger.

Volume stats answer the question 'how much did his team use him?' Efficiency stats answer 'how well did it go when they did?' Confusing the two is the oldest error in football arguments — it is how high-attempt quarterbacks on losing teams accumulate Hall-of-Fame-looking totals while moving their teams backward relative to peers.

Verdict: B, and it is not close. If A wants the crown, he can start by needing 180 fewer attempts to do less.

Player A shot 50% from the field and Player B only 45%, but the analytics guy insists B was the more efficient scorer. B had 1,800 points on 1,350 field-goal attempts and 400 free-throw attempts. A scored 1,600 on 1,600 attempts, all two-pointers, no free throws. Who's right?

The analytics guy, and the arithmetic is not subtle once you score shots by what they're worth.

Field-goal percentage treats a three and a two as identical, and ignores free throws entirely. True Shooting percentage fixes both by asking: how many points per scoring attempt, where attempts = FGA + 0.44 x FTA (the 0.44 accounts for and-ones and technicals among free-throw trips).

Player A: 1,600 points on 1,600 attempts, all twos. TS = 1600 / (2 x 1600) = .500. His 50% FG% and his efficiency are the same, because he does nothing but shoot twos.

Player B: TS = 1800 / (2 x (1350 + 0.44 x 400)) = 1800 / (2 x 1526) = 1800/3052 ≈ .590. His 45.2% from the field concealed 240 made threes (each worth an extra point) and 340 made free throws on 400 attempts — points that FG% never sees.

So B turned each scoring possession into 0.59 points per attempt-unit against A's 0.50 — roughly 18% more efficient, while looking worse in the newspaper stat. This is not a trick of a fancy metric; it is just counting points and attempts honestly.

FG% survives because it is old and simple. But any argument about scoring efficiency that starts with it is answering a question from 1975.
Wayne Gretzky scored 215 points in 1985-86. People say you can't compare that to modern 130-point seasons because 'the 80s were different.' How different, in numbers?

About 25% different in the currency points are paid in — goals.

In the mid-1980s, NHL games averaged roughly 7.9 total goals. Recent seasons average roughly 6.2. Scoring chances, goaltending, defensive systems, and equipment all moved the environment down. A point in 1986 was simply minted in a higher-inflation economy.

The standard era adjustment scales a player's scoring by the league environment: 215 x (6.2 / 7.9) ≈ 169 points in a modern-scoring season. So the apparent 85-point gap over a modern 130-point season shrinks to about 39 points — and the survival of that gap is the story.

Era adjustment is not a weapon for debunking greats; applied honestly, it separates the records that were mostly environment (many are) from the ones that were mostly the man. Gretzky's was mostly the man: he outscored his own era's second-best players by margins no modern star approaches, which is why he survives conversion into any era's currency.

The method matters more than the verdict: whenever two players from different decades are compared, first convert both into the same scoring economy, then argue. Arguing in raw points across a 25% inflation gap is not an opinion — it is an accounting error.

Our substitute striker has 12 goals and the starter has 18, but a fan account claims the sub is 'objectively the better finisher' because of goals per 90 minutes. The sub has played 1,350 minutes, the starter 2,700. Check the claim.

The arithmetic is right and the conclusion is smuggled.

Per 90 minutes: the sub scores 12 / 1350 x 90 = 0.80 goals per 90; the starter scores 18 / 2700 x 90 = 0.60 per 90. On pure rate, the sub leads. Per-90 is a real improvement over raw totals — it stops penalizing the sub for the coach's choices.

But the minutes are not interchangeable, and that is where 'objectively' dies. Substitute minutes are the kindest minutes in soccer: they come against defenders who have already run for 70 minutes, often against teams chasing a game and leaving space, and the sub himself is fresh. Starters accumulate the hard minutes — the first hour against set defenses, the away games, the matches against the top four. A rate built from easy minutes and a rate built from all minutes are not measuring the same job.

There is a sample issue too: 1,350 minutes is 15 games' worth, and goal scoring is noisy enough that a half-season of minutes cannot certify a finisher.

The honest statement is narrower and still useful: in the minutes he has been given, the sub has produced at a higher rate — which is an argument for giving him harder minutes and seeing what survives. That is how you test the claim. Declaring it settled by a rate stat is how fan accounts turn a hypothesis into a fact.
Our leadoff man led the league with 40 stolen bases and got a big contract bump for it. Another guy stole only 25. Then an analyst said the 25-steal guy was more valuable on the bases. How?

Because stolen bases are a bet, and the analyst counted the losses as well as the wins.

Your leadoff man stole 40 at a 65% success rate — that means about 40 / 0.65 ≈ 62 attempts and roughly 22 times caught stealing. The other player went 25-for-29, an 86% success rate, with only 4 caught.

Now price the outcomes. A successful steal gains a base; a caught stealing costs a base AND an out, and outs are the scarcest resource in an inning. Analysts who have run the run-expectancy math find the break-even success rate sits around 70-75%, varying with the scoring environment and game state. Above it, stealing adds runs; below it, the runner is donating outs.

At 65%, your leadoff man is below break-even: his 40 steals made highlight reels while his 22 caught-stealings quietly erased baserunners — on net, his running likely cost his team runs despite the league-leading total. The 25-for-29 runner added value in near silence, because 'didn't get thrown out' has no highlight.

This is the general shape of counting-stat fraud: the total everyone quotes records only successes. Attempts, failures, and the break-even line are where the truth lives. A league lead in a counting stat can be a liability with good marketing.
Swimming world records fell constantly in 2008 and 2009, then the rate slowed way down. Did swimmers suddenly get worse in 2010?

No — the suits got banned. Those two years are the cleanest natural experiment in sports about what a record actually measures.

In 2008-09, swimmers raced in full-body polyurethane suits that reduced drag and added buoyancy. Dozens of world records fell in that window, many by swimmers who were not otherwise the fastest of their generation. In 2010 the sport banned the suits and returned to textiles. Record-breaking slowed immediately, and some suit-era records stood for years afterward, untouchable by clean-textile swimmers who were plainly superb.

The lesson generalizes far beyond swimming. A record is a measurement of a performance under a set of conditions — equipment, surfaces, balls, bats, altitude, rules. When conditions change, the record book keeps the number and discards the context. Comparing a 2009 mark to a 2015 mark as if both were pure measures of the athlete is the same error as comparing a 1962 scoring average to a modern one without adjusting for pace.

Track's carbon-plated 'super shoes' era, tennis's string technology, baseball's ever-changing ball: every sport has suit years. The honest way to read a record book is as a joint history of athletes and their technology. The athlete supplies the engine; the era supplies some of the horsepower; the record credits the athlete with all of it.

Swimmers did not get worse in 2010. The water, in effect, got thicker — and the stopwatch finally started measuring the same sport again.
My grandfather insists quarterbacks today are 'so much more accurate' — his favorite 1970s QB completed 52% of his passes and modern guys complete 65%. Is he right?

He is right about the numbers and mostly wrong about the quarterbacks, because he is comparing each man to zero instead of to his own era.

In the 1970s, league-average completion percentage hovered around 50-51%. Defenders could maul receivers downfield until the 1978 rules changes, passing games were built on low-percentage deep shots, and 52% made his favorite roughly a point or two better than the average passer of his time.

Today the league completes about 64-65%, powered by those same rules changes plus West Coast offenses full of short, high-percentage throws. A modern quarterback at 65% is — wait for it — roughly a point or two better than the average passer of his time.

Measured against their own environments, the two men are nearly the same: modestly above-average passers. The 13-point raw gap is almost entirely the sport changing around them — rules, scheme, and strategy — not a 13-point gap in human accuracy.

This is the single most common cross-era error in sports: the baseline moves for everyone, and the raw stat credits the modern player with the movement. The fix is always the same — express performance relative to the contemporary league (points above average, a z-score, an indexed stat like passer rating relative to era). Do that, and grandfathers and grandchildren can finally argue about the same quantity: how much better than his peers each man was. On that measure, some old-timers shrink and some moderns do. The argument gets fairer and, not coincidentally, harder to win with one number.
The broadcast keeps saying our defense is terrible because it allows 400 yards a game, worst in the league. Another team allows 340. Are we really the worst?

By total yards, yes. By the thing that matters — how well the defense plays per snap — no, and the totals have the ranking backwards.

Your offense plays fast and snaps the ball constantly, so your defense faces about 75 plays a game. The other team's ball-control offense leaves its defense only about 60 plays to defend. Divide: your defense allows 400/75 ≈ 5.33 yards per play; theirs allows 340/60 ≈ 5.67 yards per play. Snap for snap, your defense is better. It just works longer shifts.

Total yards against is a workload stat wearing a quality stat's clothes. It conflates how good the defense is with how much football the other units make it play — pace, the offense's turnovers handing over short fields, and game script all leak in.

The honest defensive measures are rates: yards per play, success rate per snap, points per drive. Those ask the only question a defense can answer — what happens on the plays you actually defend.

This error is everywhere once you see it: counting stats rank exposure, rate stats rank performance. Whenever a broadcast crowns or buries a unit on a season or game total, your first move should be to ask for the denominator.

For our leadoff spot, it's between a .320 hitter with a .330 on-base percentage and a .290 hitter with a .380 OBP. The manager wants the .320 guy because 'he's the better hitter.' Talk him out of it with numbers.

Show him the outs ledger. A leadoff hitter's first job is to not make outs, because he bats more than anyone and every out he avoids is a plate appearance handed to the middle of the order.

Over 600 plate appearances: the .330 OBP hitter reaches base 198 times and makes 600 x (1 - .330) = 402 outs. The .380 OBP hitter reaches 228 times and makes 600 x (1 - .380) = 372 outs. The difference is 30 outs a season — more than an entire game's worth of outs (27) — donated back to the opposing pitchers by choosing the higher batting average.

Thirty extra times on base also means thirty more chances for your best hitters to bat with a runner aboard, thirty more pitches forced, thirty more opportunities for the running game and the extra base. Batting average conceals this because it erases walks from the record entirely: a walk does not appear in its numerator or denominator, so the stat literally cannot see the .380 man's most common way of reaching base.

The .320 hitter may well be the better pure hitter — put a pitch in the zone and he is more likely to hit it. But 'better hitter' by average and 'better leadoff man' are different claims, and for the leadoff job the relevant skill is reaching base by any legal means. Average is the wrong instrument for the job. OBP is the job description, written as a number.
The big projection system says my team will win 92 games. They won 84. Was the projection just wrong?

Probably not — and the way you're reading it guarantees you'll think every projection is wrong.

A projection of 92 wins is not a prediction that the team will win 92 games. It is the center of a distribution: the system's best single summary of thousands of simulated seasons. Honest projection systems, checked against history, miss a team's actual win total by on the order of 8 wins in a typical year — in either direction. A team projected at 92 landing anywhere from the low 80s to 100 is the system working as designed, not failing.

Where does the spread come from? Mostly things no March model can know: injuries to players projected for full seasons, a closer's elbow, a prospect arriving in June instead of never, the trade deadline reshaping two rosters. Performance uncertainty on top of playing-time uncertainty compounds into that wide band.

The right way to grade a projection system is across all 30 teams and many seasons: are its 92-win teams winning about 92 on average? Are its misses symmetric? A system that projects your team at 92 and is calibrated is doing excellent work even when your team wins 84 — your team is one draw from its distribution.

The broadcast habit of reading a projection as a promise, then mocking it in September, is like mocking a weather forecaster who said 70% chance of rain on a day it stayed dry. Grade the forecaster on a hundred forecasts, and the projection on thirty teams. Single outcomes grade nothing but luck.

The betting line says my team is favored by 7. My brother says that means the experts think we'll win by exactly 7, and he's furious when we 'only' win by 3. What does a point spread actually represent?

Tell your brother the spread is a price, not a prophecy — and the distinction explains both the line and his fury.

A sportsbook sets the spread to balance betting on both sides, because it profits from the commission, not from being right about football. The closing line therefore represents the betting market's collective median expectation: half the expected outcomes above 7, half below. It is the wisdom of a crowd with money at stake, which makes it a genuinely sharp estimate — and still just a center of a very wide distribution.

Game margins are dispersed widely around any line. A team favored by 7 wins by exactly 7 only occasionally; it wins by 3, by 17, and loses outright in fat slices of the distribution. Roughly speaking, a 7-point favorite wins the game somewhere around three times in four — which means it loses one time in four, and 'only' winning by 3 is one of the most ordinary outcomes on the menu.

The spread's real information content is comparative: it tells you the market rates your team about a touchdown better than the opponent, on this field, this week, with these injuries. Treating it as a promised margin is like treating a stock price as a promise of next year's earnings — it is a consensus estimate, updated by people betting real money, and it is wrong in detail almost every single game.

Your brother's team covered his emotional spread — they won. The market's spread was never a contract.

Our quarterback put up huge numbers in the fourth quarter last week — 180 yards and two touchdowns. A writer called it a 'statement performance.' We were down 24 when the quarter started. How should I read those stats?

As real yards recorded in a fake game. The fourth quarter of a blowout is a different sport from the first three, and counting stats cannot tell them apart — which is exactly the problem.

Down 24, the defense's goals change completely. It happily concedes 12-yard completions in the middle of the field, keeps everything in front, protects the sideline and the end zone, and trades yards for clock. The quarterback is no longer solving the defense; he is accepting its gifts. His 180 yards were, in large part, the defense's strategy working as intended.

Context-aware stats exist precisely to catch this. Win Probability Added assigns almost no credit to plays that move a team from a 1% chance to a 3% chance — the two touchdowns barely dented the outcome, so they barely register. That is why the same writer's 'statement performance' does not appear in the WPA leaders, and why garbage-time production rarely predicts anything about next week, when the defense will be trying again.

The honest summary of his quarter: he played well against a defense that was no longer contesting the plays he was completing. That is worth something — backups and bad quarterbacks fail even at that — but it is evidence about his floor, not a statement about his ceiling.
